Name: information_burst_reasoning
Title: Bits Per Step: Do Information-Density Bursts Cause LLM Reasoning Failures, and Can Pacing Them Fix It?
Short Hypothesis: LLM reasoning failures are causally linked to information-density bursts — individual reasoning steps that try to transmit too many bits at once (violating local Uniform Information Density) — rather than merely being correlated with them; a locatable internal 'information-pacing' signal governs how many bits a step emits, and causally reducing bursts at high-risk steps (by inducing the model to decompose them into more, lower-density steps) improves reasoning more than length-matched extra computation.
Related Work: The Uniform Information Density (UID) hypothesis (Jaeger 2008; Genzel & Charniak 2001) posits humans pace information evenly. Recent LLM work (Gwak, Son & Kim, ACL 2025; 'Revisiting UID in LLM Reasoning Traces', 2025) computes entropy-based stepwise information-density metrics and finds a robust pattern: correct reasoning is locally uniform (smooth step-to-step transitions) but globally non-uniform, and that information-density spikes/bursts predict incorrect traces — they use this as a trace-SELECTION signal (reranking many samples). Entropy-rate work (Revisiting Entropy Rate Constancy, 2023; Constant Conditional Entropy, 2013) studies text-level uniformity but not reasoning. Crucially, ALL existing LLM-UID work is (1) purely correlational — it selects among traces the model already produced but never intervenes to change pacing, (2) treats information density as a passive readout with no internal locus, and (3) offers no causal test that bursts CAUSE failure rather than co-occur with hard steps. My prior proposals covered linguistic relativity, cognitive-analogy transfers, tokenization granularity, and difficulty-gated language-agnostic steering — none address information-density pacing, bursts, or a bits-per-step controller. We uniquely (a) causally test whether an induced information burst at a step degrades reasoning and whether burst-reduction repairs it, (b) locate an internal information-pacing signal, and (c) turn UID from a reranking heuristic into a training-free, single-pass pacing intervention, with a high-stakes clinical instance.
Abstract: A striking recent finding is that an LLM's step-by-step reasoning is locally smooth but globally uneven in information density, and that sharp information-density bursts — steps that pack many bits into few tokens — reliably flag incorrect reasoning. Existing work exploits this only correlationally, as a signal for reranking many sampled traces. We ask the causal question: do information bursts CAUSE reasoning failures, and can pacing them fix reasoning in a single pass? We propose that each reasoning step has a controllable information budget, that overloading a step (a burst) is a proximal cause of downstream errors, and that an LLM carries a locatable internal 'information-pacing' signal governing how many bits it commits per step. We test three claims. First, bursts are causal, not incidental: experimentally inducing a burst (forcing the model to compress a multi-inference step into one dense token span) raises error rates beyond matched-difficulty controls, and correct traces avoid bursts at genuinely hard steps. Second, pacing is a locatable internal quantity: a probe reads a step's committed information load from hidden states before the step completes, predicting impending bursts and errors. Third, pacing is a steerable, useful lever: at high-risk (predicted-burst) steps only, we causally reduce density by inducing decomposition into more, lower-density steps, and show this Burst-Aware Pacing improves accuracy more than length-matched extra reasoning, blanket 'think more' prompting, or random-step decomposition. We evaluate on math, logic, and multi-hop QA across several open-weight models, plus a high-stakes clinical-reasoning instance where a single overloaded inference step silently produces a wrong diagnosis. Our work reframes information density from a passive reranking signal into a causal, controllable resource for machine reasoning.
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use five frozen open-weight models -- Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights (logistic or ridge regression on frozen hidden states). Decoding is greedy for the primary condition and temperature 0.7 for any sampled condition, each sampled/steered run repeated over seeds 0, 1, 2. All effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs) over 1000 item-level resamples, and behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts for model and item, written (1|model)+(1|item). Reasoning traces are segmented into steps at sentence/newline boundaries; per-step information density is mean token surprisal under the generating model plus a bits-per-inference measure normalized by content tokens, following the stepwise Uniform-Information-Density metrics of Gwak et al. 2025; a burst is a step whose density exceeds that item's within-trace running-median density by more than 1.5 standard deviations.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Bursts causally degrade reasoning rather than merely co-occurring with hard steps): Tests whether a forced information-density burst at a step raises error beyond what step difficulty alone predicts. Data: 500 items sampled from the GSM8K test split (1,319 available), 500 from the MATH test split (5,000 available) stratified across difficulty levels 1-5, 400 synthetic deductive-logic chains we construct (modus-ponens chaining templates, branching depth 2-6, answers auto-checkable), and 400 questions sampled from the 2WikiMultiHopQA dev set (12,576 available), 1,800 items total; these sizes give a few hundred items per task for stable step-level mixed-effects estimates across five models while staying within a single-GPU-week budget. On items each model first solves correctly under free reasoning, four systems are compared: (i) free baseline; (ii) burst-injection -- re-prompt with a structural constraint forcing one target multi-inference step to be compressed into a single dense token span, total reasoning content held constant; (iii) length-matched control -- add equal token count elsewhere without compressing the target step; (iv) decomposition control -- expand the same step into more, lower-density steps. Decisive metric first: final-answer accuracy of burst-injection minus the length-matched control at genuinely hard steps (top difficulty tercile), from mixed-effects logistic regression accuracy ~ condition * step_difficulty + (1|model)+(1|item); secondary metric: error-localization rate (fraction of induced errors whose first wrong step is the injected step or its direct consequence). Convincing result: burst-injection is at least 5 percentage points below the length-matched control with a CI excluding 0, at least 60% of induced errors localize to the injected step, and the decomposition control sits at or above free baseline. Indecision band: a burst-minus-length-matched gap within +/-2 points (CI overlapping 0) is uninformative -- compression is not separable from added content at our power, and we report that rather than a causal claim. Negative result: if burst-injection does not fall below the length-matched control (gap <= 0), bursts are not a distinct causal factor beyond difficulty and length, and H1's causal claim collapses to the prior correlational finding; only injection-compliant trials (verified content preservation) are analyzed.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- A locatable pre-emission information-pacing signal): Tests whether hidden states at a step boundary, before the step's content is emitted, encode the impending step's information load. Data: reuse the traces from Experiment 1, split 70/30 by item into probe-train and held-out sets. At each step-boundary position we extract residual-stream activations at every layer and train (only the probe is trainable) a ridge regressor to predict the impending step's density and a logistic probe to predict whether it will be a burst, reporting per-layer held-out AUROC and R-squared; baselines are boundary token-entropy, post-hoc per-step surprisal, and verbalized confidence elicited from the model. Decisive metric first: held-out burst-prediction AUROC from pre-step hidden states; secondary: Spearman correlation between an item's mean pre-step burst probability and final-answer error. Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.70 on held-out items, exceeding the best baseline by >= 0.05, with pre-step burst probability predicting item error at Spearman rho >= 0.2 (CI excludes 0). Indecision band: AUROC in 0.55-0.65 is a weak signal we cannot separate from generic entropy, and we would decline to claim a dedicated pacing readout. Negative result: AUROC ~ 0.5 or no gain over the entropy baseline means no locatable pre-emission pacing signal exists, refuting H2 and leaving pacing a post-hoc description.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- Burst-Aware Pacing beats length-matched extra computation): Tests whether reducing density only at predicted-burst steps improves accuracy more than simply computing more. Data: the same 1,800 items. Five single-pass systems at matched token budgets: no-intervention; blanket "think step by step / think more" prompting; random-step decomposition (matched number of interventions and tokens); a Uniform-Information-Density reranking baseline (Gwak et al. 2025, cost-matched to the same token budget); and Burst-Aware Pacing -- flag high-risk steps online with the Experiment-2 pre-step probe (or a surprisal-threshold proxy) and inject a decomposition instruction only at flagged steps. Decisive metric first: accuracy at matched token budget, reported as an accuracy-versus-token-cost curve, with the primary contrast Burst-Aware Pacing minus random-step decomposition; secondary: accuracy versus blanket prompting and versus reranking at equal cost. Convincing result: Burst-Aware Pacing matches or exceeds blanket prompting and reranking at equal or lower token cost and beats random-step decomposition by >= 3 points (CI excludes 0), showing that where you pace matters, not merely that you pace. Indecision band: Burst-Aware Pacing within +/-2 points of random-step decomposition means placement is not demonstrably load-bearing though pacing may still help. Negative result: no gain over no-intervention, or a deficit versus blanket prompting at equal cost, refutes H3's usefulness claim.

Experiment 4 (H1 and H3 -- High-stakes clinical instance): Tests whether a single overloaded clinical inference step silently causes misdiagnosis and whether Burst-Aware Pacing mitigates it. Data: 300 differential-diagnosis vignettes adapted from MedQA (USMLE, 12,723 questions) fine-distinction items plus constructed vignettes in which multiple clinical inferences can be compressed into one dense assertion; we use 300 because expert spot-checking of ground truth is costly and 300 supports the paired burst/pace contrasts. Systems: free baseline, burst-injection at the pivotal clinical step, and Burst-Aware Pacing. Decisive metric first: confident-misdiagnosis rate (wrong diagnosis emitted with high stated confidence); secondary: overall diagnostic accuracy. Convincing result: burst-injection raises confident misdiagnosis and Burst-Aware Pacing lowers it by >= 5 points on fine-distinction cases (CIs exclude 0). Indecision band: a pacing effect within +/-2 points is inconclusive for high-stakes transfer. Negative result: no movement means the pacing lever does not transfer to high-stakes reasoning, bounding the claim to benign benchmarks.

Experiment 5 (H2 and H3 -- Causal pacing-direction steering, mechanistic depth): Tests whether directly lowering the internal pacing signal reproduces the Burst-Aware Pacing benefit without any decomposition prompt. Data: the 1,800 items from Experiment 1. We derive a difference-in-means "pacing" direction from high-density-minus-low-density step-boundary activation contrasts (matched content) at the best probe layer, then steer minus-direction at flagged steps; controls are random-direction steering of matched norm and no-steer. Decisive metric first: accuracy gain of minus-direction steering over random-direction steering, with a dose-response sweep over steering magnitude; secondary: specificity (accuracy change on easy items, which must stay within 1 point, and fluency by perplexity). Convincing result: a monotonic dose-response and a >= 3-point accuracy gain over random-direction steering with preserved easy-item accuracy. Indecision band: a gain within +/-2 points of random-direction steering leaves the direction unproven, in which case the prompt-based Burst-Aware Pacing and the burst-injection causal result stand independently. Negative result: no benefit from a clean direction, or benefit indistinguishable from random steering, means the internal pacing quantity is not a usable causal lever even if it is readable.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Surprisal-based information density is model-internal and confounded with step difficulty — hard steps are naturally denser; mitigated by matched-difficulty controls, by testing the burst-injection vs length-matched vs decomposition CONTROLS (isolating compression from content/length), and by error-localization checks that show the injected step specifically drives failure. (2) Burst injection via prompting may be non-compliant or change content, not just density; we verify compliance, hold reasoning content constant, and analyze only compliant trials. (3) The pacing probe may capture generic difficulty/confidence rather than a genuine bits-per-step controller; mitigated by held-out validation, comparison to confidence/entropy baselines, the pre-step (before-emission) prediction requirement, and random-direction steering controls. (4) BAP's decomposition prompt could help simply by adding tokens/'thinking time'; the random-step-decomposition and cost-matched reranking baselines isolate the value of WHERE pacing is applied. (5) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (6) Global-non-uniformity findings (Gwak et al.) suggest LLM reasoning legitimately needs some bursts; our claim is specifically about bursts at HARD/pivotal steps, and a null result (bursts are benign or even helpful) would itself be informative, refining when UID applies to machine reasoning. (7) The optional steering variant depends on a clean pacing direction; if unavailable, the prompt-based BAP and the causal burst-injection results stand independently. (8) The UID framing is operationalized information-theoretically and behaviorally, not as a claim of human-like production planning.

Name: self_invented_shorthand
Title: Shorthand for Thought: Does an LLM's Self-Invented Compressed Notation Help Reasoning Up to a Compression Cliff?
Short Hypothesis: When a frozen LLM is induced to invent and reuse its own compressed private notation (a self-shorthand) for intermediate results during multi-step reasoning, task accuracy follows an inverted-U over compression pressure: light shorthand improves reasoning (working-memory offloading) while aggressive shorthand collapses it at a 'compression cliff' where the model can no longer decode its own symbols; the ability to decode self-invented symbols is a locatable, steerable internal signal whose strength predicts and causally gates where the cliff falls.
Related Work: Emergent-communication work shows noise catalyzes compositional codes (Catalytic Role of Noise, 2021), discrete emergent language is more robust and generalizable than continuous features (Emergence of Machine Language, 2022), and compositionality aids transmissibility but not raw generalization (Compositionality and Generalization, 2020). Inter-LLM activation-communication work (Communicating Activations Between LM Agents, 2025; OPTi-MACS, 2023) shows non-natural-language message representations can outperform natural language between DISTINCT agents with TRAINED or fixed protocols. Latent/implicit-reasoning work (Coconut, 2024) removes verbalization entirely. Notation-effect work notes format changes reasoning, and my prior proposals covered tokenization granularity, naming-as-chunking, and information-density pacing. NONE test whether a SINGLE frozen model, in-context and without training, benefits from inventing and reusing its OWN compressed notation for its own downstream use, whether this benefit is non-monotonic with a self-decodability cliff, or whether self-symbol decodability is a locatable/steerable internal quantity that gates the cliff. We uniquely turn 'compressed private language' from a multi-agent trained protocol into a single-model, training-free, mechanistically-characterized reasoning resource with a predicted compression cliff.
Abstract: Human experts invent shorthand — abbreviations, private notations, compressed diagrams — that let them offload working memory and reason faster, but only as long as they can still decode what they wrote. We ask whether large language models exhibit the same double-edged relationship between compressed language and intelligence. In a single frozen model, we induce the model to invent and reuse its own compressed private notation for intermediate results across a multi-step reasoning task, and vary the compression pressure from verbose natural language to aggressive symbol-dense shorthand. Our central prediction is a compression cliff: accuracy follows an inverted-U over compression — light shorthand improves reasoning by offloading working memory over long contexts, while aggressive shorthand collapses performance once the model can no longer reliably decode its own symbols. We further predict the cliff is not fixed by the notation's raw density but by the model's self-decodability — its ability to recover the meaning of symbols it just coined. Mechanistically, we test whether self-decodability is a locatable internal signal: a probe reading whether a coined symbol is still bound to its referent should predict impending decoding failure and the cliff location, and steering this decoding signal should move the cliff, letting the model tolerate more compression before collapse. Across several open-weight models and reasoning domains (math, multi-hop QA, state-tracking), plus a high-stakes clinical hand-off instance where compressed notation causes silent errors, we quantify the inverted-U, the self-decodability-to-cliff link, and steering controllability, reframing self-invented compressed language as a controllable lever on — and a hidden failure mode of — machine reasoning.
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use five frozen open-weight models -- Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights (logistic or ridge regression on frozen hidden states). Decoding is greedy for the primary condition and temperature 0.7 for any sampled/spot-check condition, each such run repeated over seeds 0, 1, 2. All effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs) over 1000 item-level resamples, and behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts for model and item, written (1|model)+(1|item). "Self-shorthand" means a compact private notation the model is instructed to invent for its own intermediate results and then reuse by referring back to its own symbols.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Self-shorthand produces an inverted-U over compression pressure with a compression cliff): Tests whether task accuracy rises then falls as compression pressure increases. Data: three multi-step tasks -- 300 multi-step arithmetic items sampled from the GSM8K test split (1,319 available), 300 multi-hop QA items over 3-6 facts sampled from the 2WikiMultiHopQA dev set (12,576 available), and 300 synthetic state-tracking items we construct (entity-attribute updates over long contexts, answers auto-checkable) -- 900 base items, each run at four compression levels for 3,600 conditions; 300/task/level is the smallest sample giving stable per-model cliff estimates within a single-GPU-week budget. Compression levels: L0 verbose natural language (baseline), L1 short abbreviations, L2 coined single-token symbols, L3 aggressive symbol-dense shorthand (maximal abbreviation, dropped connectives); format is enforced and symbol reuse verified so only compliant trials count. Decisive metric first: final-answer accuracy as a function of compression level, tested for an inverted-U via mixed-effects logistic regression accuracy ~ compression_level (as ordered factor) * context_length + (1|model)+(1|item), with the per-model/per-task cliff located as the level of first significant drop; secondary: the compression_level x context_length interaction (offloading benefit should be largest on long-context items). Convincing result: mean accuracy rises from L0 to L1 or L2 by >= 3 points (CI excludes 0), then falls at L3 by >= 5 points from its peak (CI excludes 0), with the benefit significantly larger on the top context-length tercile. Indecision band: any level-to-level change within +/-2 points (CI overlapping 0) is treated as flat; if both the rise and the fall land in this band the inverted-U is unsupported. Negative result: monotonic decline with no L1/L2 benefit still supports a compression cliff (partial support), while flat accuracy across all levels refutes H1 entirely; a monotonic-decline outcome is reported as such rather than reframed.

Experiment 2 (H1 confounds -- Isolating self-authored reused compression from token count and abbreviation per se): Tests that the benefit comes from reusing self-invented compressed memory, not fewer tokens or the act of abbreviating. Data: the same 900 base items. Systems: L0 baseline; a length-matched control that equalizes total token budget across levels; a fixed-external-code control that supplies a provided abbreviation legend instead of self-invented symbols; and a no-reuse control that writes shorthand but never refers back. Decisive metric first: accuracy difference between self-invented-reused shorthand and each control at the L1/L2 peak; secondary: accuracy under length-matching to rule out "fewer tokens to attend to". Convincing result: self-invented-reused shorthand exceeds the no-reuse and fixed-external-code controls by >= 3 points at the peak (CIs exclude 0) and the benefit survives length-matching. Indecision band: differences within +/-2 points mean self-authorship and reuse are not separable from generic abbreviation at our power. Negative result: if the fixed-external-code or no-reuse control matches self-shorthand, the effect is not about self-invented reusable compression, weakening H1's mechanism.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- Self-decodability is a locatable signal that tracks the cliff better than raw density): Tests whether the model's ability to decode its own symbols predicts the cliff. Data: the reference points in the L0-L3 traces from Experiment 1, split 70/30 by item. Two measures at each symbol reference: an interleaved behavioral spot-check ("what does <symbol> stand for?") on a held-out subset, and a linear probe (only probe trainable) on hidden states at the reference token decoding the bound referent, per-layer held-out AUROC. Decisive metric first: per-layer held-out decoding AUROC and its drop across compression levels; secondary: model comparison of two predictors of per-item accuracy -- a density-only baseline versus a self-decodability-based predictor (nested-model likelihood-ratio / delta-AUROC). Convincing result: decodability drops sharply at the located cliff level (>= 0.10 AUROC decrease from L1/L2 to L3, CI excludes 0), per-item decodability predicts per-item error at Spearman rho >= 0.2, and the decodability predictor beats the density-only predictor of accuracy (delta-AUROC >= 0.05, CI excludes 0). Indecision band: a decodability-versus-density predictor gap within +/-0.03 AUROC means the cliff cannot be attributed to decodability over density. Negative result: if raw density predicts the cliff as well as decodability, or decodability does not fall at the cliff, H2's decodability-gates-the-cliff claim fails.

Experiment 4 (H2 -- Steering the decoding signal moves the cliff): Tests whether the decoding signal is causal and steerable. Data: the same reference points. We derive a difference-in-means "symbol-binding/decoding" direction from decodable-minus-failed-decode reference contrasts at the best probe layer; systems are plus-direction steering, minus-direction steering, random-direction steering of matched norm, and no-steer. Decisive metric first: shift in the located cliff level under plus-direction steering versus random-direction and no-steer (does the model tolerate a denser level before collapse?); secondary: minus-direction induced early collapse at mild compression, plus specificity (L0 accuracy within 1 point, fluency by perplexity). Convincing result: plus-direction steering pushes the cliff to a higher compression level (or raises L3 accuracy by >= 3 points over random-direction, CI excludes 0) while minus-direction lowers accuracy at L1/L2, both with preserved L0 accuracy and a monotonic dose-response. Indecision band: cliff-shift effects within +/-2 accuracy points of random-direction steering leave the direction unproven. Negative result: no cliff movement beyond random steering means self-decodability, even if readable, is not a usable causal gate, and the behavioral inverted-U (Experiment 1) stands alone.

Experiment 5 (H1 and H2 -- High-stakes clinical hand-off instance): Tests whether aggressive self-shorthand silently drops a decision-relevant detail and whether decoding-direction steering mitigates it. Data: 300 clinical hand-off / note-summarization vignettes adapted from MedQA (USMLE, 12,723 questions) and constructed hand-off cases, where the model compresses a patient case into shorthand and then answers a fine-grained downstream question; 300 supports paired contrasts under expert spot-checking. Systems: L0 verbose, L3 aggressive shorthand, and L3 with plus-direction decoding steering. Decisive metric first: confident-error rate on the downstream question (wrong answer with high stated confidence) at L3 versus L0; secondary: recovery under steering. Convincing result: L3 raises confident downstream error over L0 and plus-direction steering reduces it by >= 5 points (CIs exclude 0). Indecision band: an L3-versus-L0 gap within +/-2 points is inconclusive for high-stakes transfer. Negative result: no L3 degradation means aggressive self-shorthand is safe here, bounding the failure-mode claim to benign tasks.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Instruction-tuned models may refuse or inconsistently follow the self-shorthand instruction, or covertly keep verbose reasoning; we enforce and verify symbol reuse, analyze only compliant trials, and include base-model variants. (2) The offloading benefit may be absent if models already handle long contexts well, flattening the inverted-U to a monotonic decline; a monotonic result (no benefit, only a cliff) is itself informative and the cliff/self-decodability mechanism still holds. (3) Compression confounds with token count and content; mitigated by length-matched budgets, fixed-external-code and no-reuse controls, and the decodability-vs-density predictor comparison. (4) Self-decodability spot-checks may perturb the reasoning trace; we use a held-out subset and the non-invasive hidden-state probe as the primary measure. (5) The decoding direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence; addressed by matched decodable/failed contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and L0 specificity checks. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) The 'shorthand for thought' framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like working memory.

Name: reasoning_register_shift
Title: Simpler Sentences, Deeper Thought: Do LLMs Downshift Their Own Syntax When Reasoning Gets Hard?
Short Hypothesis: When reasoning becomes difficult, an LLM spontaneously reduces the syntactic complexity of its own generated language (a 'register downshift'), reallocating capacity from fluent surface form to computation; this downshift is a readable, per-step signal of reasoning difficulty and impending error, and causally forcing high-syntactic-complexity output at hard steps degrades reasoning while inducing simpler output syntax at hard steps improves it.
Related Work: Prior work links syntactic complexity to reasoning only for the INPUT or TRAINING data. 'Syntactic Blind Spots' (2025) shows higher Dependency-Locality-Theory (DLT) complexity of the PROBLEM STATEMENT raises math-error rates, and rephrasing to simpler syntax fixes errors. CIRS / 'When Do Program-of-Thoughts Work' (2023/2024) find an optimal AST/cyclomatic complexity of code TRAINING data for reasoning gains. 'Understanding Syntax in LLMs' (2025) and ID-of-representation work (2026) characterize how models process complex syntax, and 'Reasoning in LLMs: A Geometric Perspective' (2024) links intrinsic dimension to reasoning. Multi-dimensional gCoT-quality studies (2026) measure trace quality but not self-generated syntactic complexity as a function of difficulty. Critically, NO prior work studies the syntactic complexity of the model's OWN generated reasoning trace as a dynamic, self-regulated variable, tests whether it downshifts with difficulty, uses it as a difficulty/error signal, or causally intervenes on output-syntax complexity at the step level. My own prior proposals covered information-density pacing (bits per step), private-speech length dynamics, and tokenization granularity, but none address the syntactic (dependency-structure) complexity of self-generated language or a register-downshift-under-load account. We uniquely flip the direction from input-syntax->reasoning to reasoning-difficulty->output-syntax, and add a Location + Causal Intervention mechanism.
Abstract: Existing work shows that syntactically complex problem statements make LLMs reason worse, and that there is an optimal syntactic complexity in reasoning-oriented training data. We ask a complementary, unexplored question: what governs the syntactic complexity of the language an LLM PRODUCES while it reasons, and does it matter? Drawing on the human observation that speakers simplify their syntax under cognitive load, we hypothesize a reasoning register shift: as a reasoning sub-step becomes hard, the model spontaneously downshifts the syntactic complexity of its own generated tokens, trading fluent surface form for computational capacity. We make three claims. First, downshift is real and graded: per-step syntactic complexity of a model's chain-of-thought (measured by dependency-tree depth, Dependency-Locality-Theory integration cost, and clause embedding) drops at genuinely hard steps, and its magnitude tracks step difficulty. Second, downshift is diagnostic: per-step output-syntax complexity predicts step-level errors and final-answer correctness, providing a lightweight, decode-only self-monitoring signal that complements confidence and entropy. Third, downshift is causal, not incidental: forcing the model to emit high-complexity (elaborate, deeply-embedded) syntax at hard steps degrades reasoning, while inducing simpler syntax at hard steps improves it, and these effects are mediated by a locatable internal 'syntactic-elaboration' signal that can be steered to move the register up or down. We test these on multilingual math, logic, and multi-hop QA across several open-weight models, plus a high-stakes clinical-reasoning instance where syntactically elaborate self-generated reasoning silently raises diagnostic error. Our work reframes an LLM's own linguistic form as a controllable resource that competes with, and can sabotage, its reasoning.
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use five frozen open-weight models -- Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights on frozen hidden states. Decoding is greedy for the primary condition and temperature 0.7 for any sampled condition, each such run over seeds 0, 1, 2. Effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap CIs over 1000 item-level resamples; behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts (1|model)+(1|item). Traces are segmented into steps at sentence/newline boundaries. For each step's generated text we compute a Syntactic Complexity Score (SCS) from an off-the-shelf dependency parser (Stanza, with UDPipe as a second parser for robustness): mean dependency-tree depth, Dependency-Locality-Theory integration cost, clause-embedding/subordination ratio, and mean dependency length; parsers are validated on each target language and results reported across all four metrics. Tasks are rendered in 3-4 typologically diverse languages (English, Spanish, Turkish, Chinese).

Experiment 1 (H1 -- The model spontaneously downshifts its own output syntax as difficulty rises): Tests whether per-step SCS drops at harder steps. Data: 500 items from the GSM8K test split (1,319 available), 500 from the MATH test split (5,000 available, level-stratified), 400 synthetic deductive-logic chains we construct (depth 2-6, auto-checkable), and 400 items from the 2WikiMultiHopQA dev set (12,576 available), 1,800 base items each rendered in each language; these sizes give a few hundred items/task/language for stable step-level estimates within a single-GPU-week budget. Difficulty proxies per step: per-step surprisal, operation complexity for math, and hop index for QA. Decisive metric first: the step_difficulty coefficient in mixed-effects regression SCS ~ step_difficulty + step_position + (1|model)+(1|item), pooled across parsers and languages; secondary: robustness of the sign across the four SCS metrics and across parsers. Convincing result: a negative, statistically reliable difficulty coefficient (CI excludes 0) consistent in sign across >= 3 of 4 SCS metrics and both parsers, with a position control ruling out that SCS merely tracks step index. Indecision band: a standardized difficulty coefficient whose CI lies within +/-0.05 is treated as no downshift. Negative result: a null or positive coefficient means the model does not simplify its own syntax under load, refuting H1 and dissociating LLMs from the human load-induced-simplification account.

Experiment 2 (H1 -- Downshift tracks genuine difficulty, not step length or position): Tests that SCS drops at genuine hard/error-recovery steps beyond position and length confounds. Data: the same 1,800 items; on items solved correctly under free reasoning, we inject a controlled error or truncate at a step to create genuine error-recovery/hard steps, matched to easy steps at the same position and length. Decisive metric first: within-item SCS difference at error-recovery/hard steps minus matched easy steps at equal position and length; secondary: token-length-matched re-analysis. Convincing result: SCS is lower at genuine hard steps by a reliable margin (CI excludes 0) after matching position and length. Indecision band: a matched SCS difference within +/-0.05 standardized units is uninformative. Negative result: no SCS drop after matching means the Experiment-1 effect was a length/position artifact.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- Per-step output-syntax complexity is diagnostic of errors): Tests whether SCS predicts step-level and final errors. Data: the traces above, split 70/30 by item. A lightweight probe (only probe trainable) is trained on per-step SCS features to predict step-level error and final correctness. Baselines: token entropy, verbalized confidence, per-step surprisal, and the information-density burst signal (density above within-trace running median). Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC for final-correctness prediction from SCS features; secondary: step-level error AUROC and delta-AUROC over each baseline. Convincing result: SCS-based AUROC >= 0.65 and exceeds the best baseline by >= 0.05 (CI excludes 0). Indecision band: AUROC in 0.55-0.62 or a delta over baselines within +/-0.03 means SCS carries no diagnostic value beyond existing signals. Negative result: AUROC ~ 0.5 refutes H2's diagnostic claim.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- Forcing high-complexity syntax at hard steps degrades reasoning; simpler syntax helps): Tests the causal, content-matched syntax effect. Data: the same 1,800 items. Via strict-format prompting, each step is forced into HIGH-complexity syntax (elaborate, deeply embedded, subordinated), LOW-complexity syntax (short, flat, coordinated), or FREE baseline, with reasoning content held constant (same operations required) and SCS verified to actually differ; a length-matched control equalizes token count across conditions. Decisive metric first: the syntax_condition x step_difficulty interaction on accuracy from mixed-effects logistic regression accuracy ~ syntax_condition * step_difficulty + (1|model)+(1|item); secondary: main effects at hard versus easy steps. Convincing result: HIGH-complexity syntax lowers accuracy disproportionately at hard steps (>= 4 points below FREE, CI excludes 0) and LOW-complexity helps at hard steps (>= 3 points above FREE), while both are within 2 points of FREE on easy steps, and the effect survives length-matching (isolating syntactic form from verbosity). Indecision band: interaction effects within +/-2 points (CI overlapping 0) mean output-syntax form does not modulate reasoning. Negative result: no interaction, or equal effects on easy and hard steps, refutes H3's causal syntax claim; only compliant, content-preserving trials are analyzed.

Experiment 5 (H3 -- Difficulty-gated simplification beats blanket and random-gated simplification): Tests that where you simplify matters. Data: the same items. Systems at matched token budget: no-intervention; blanket simplification (every step); random-gated simplification (matched intervention count at random steps); and Register-Gated Simplification (induce LOW-complexity syntax only at steps flagged hard by a surprisal threshold or the Experiment-3 probe). Decisive metric first: accuracy at matched token cost, primary contrast Register-Gated minus random-gated; secondary: Register-Gated versus blanket at equal cost. Convincing result: Register-Gated matches or exceeds blanket at lower cost and beats random-gated by >= 3 points (CI excludes 0). Indecision band: within +/-2 points of random-gated means placement is not load-bearing. Negative result: no gain over no-intervention refutes the practical value of H3.

Experiment 6 (H3 -- A locatable, steerable syntactic-elaboration signal mediates downshift): Tests the mechanism. Data: matched high-SCS-minus-low-SCS content-matched generation contrasts yield a difference-in-means "syntactic-elaboration" direction (per-layer probe AUROC, held-out validated). Systems: minus-direction steering at hard steps (predict accuracy gain), plus-direction (predict degradation), random-direction of matched norm, and no-steer. Decisive metric first: accuracy change from minus-direction steering at hard steps versus random-direction; secondary: whether the elaboration signal engages more at easy than hard steps (mediating downshift), per-item elaboration-signal-to-SCS/error Spearman correlation, dose-response, and specificity (easy-item accuracy within 1 point, fluency preserved). Convincing result: minus-direction steering raises hard-step accuracy by >= 3 points over random-direction (CI excludes 0) with monotonic dose-response and preserved easy-item accuracy, and the signal is higher at easy steps. Indecision band: steering effects within +/-2 points of random-direction leave the direction unproven; behavioral Experiments 4-5 then stand alone. Negative result: no steerable effect means the elaboration direction is not causal.

Experiment 7 (H3 -- High-stakes clinical instance): Tests whether elaborate self-generated reasoning raises misdiagnosis and register-gated simplification mitigates it. Data: 300 differential-diagnosis vignettes adapted from MedQA (USMLE, 12,723 questions) fine-distinction items; 300 supports paired contrasts under expert spot-checking. Systems: FREE, forced HIGH-complexity syntax, and Register-Gated Simplification. Decisive metric first: confident-misdiagnosis rate on fine-distinction cases under HIGH-complexity versus FREE; secondary: mitigation under Register-Gated. Convincing result: HIGH-complexity raises confident misdiagnosis and Register-Gated lowers it by >= 5 points (CIs exclude 0). Indecision band: gaps within +/-2 points are inconclusive for high-stakes transfer. Negative result: no effect bounds the claim to benign benchmarks.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) SCS may be confounded with step length and difficulty (hard steps are shorter/simpler for many reasons); mitigated by length-matched controls, testing the syntax x difficulty INTERACTION rather than raw drops, position controls, and the content-matched forced-syntax and steering interventions that isolate syntactic form from content. (2) Dependency parsers are imperfect on model-generated and multilingual text; we use multiple complexity metrics and parsers, validate on the target languages, and report robustness. (3) Forcing high/low syntax via prompting may be non-compliant or covertly change content; we verify SCS actually shifts, hold operations constant, and analyze only compliant trials. (4) Instruction-tuned models may resist syntactic manipulation or already reason robustly, flattening effects; we include base variants, calibrate difficulty to mid-range, and test multiple models. (5) The elaboration direction may entangle with generic difficulty/verbosity rather than syntax per se; mitigated by content-matched high/low-SCS contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and easy-item specificity checks. (6) Effects may be small or model-/language-specific; we report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (output-syntax complexity does not affect reasoning, or does not downshift under load) is itself informative: it would show an LLM's self-generated linguistic form is decoupled from its reasoning, dissociating LLMs from the human load-induced-simplification account. (8) The 'register shift under cognitive load' framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like processing limits.

Name: premature_disambiguation_branching
Title: Committing Too Soon: Does an LLM Silently Collapse Ambiguous Inputs to One Reading, and Can Keeping Interpretation Branches Alive Fix It?
Short Hypothesis: When a genuinely ambiguous input admits multiple valid readings, an LLM silently disambiguates to a single interpretation early in its reasoning and then reasons confidently down that one branch, discarding the alternatives before it has evidence to choose; the number of interpretation branches the model keeps 'alive' is a readable, causal internal signal, and inducing the model to maintain competing branches (rather than abstain) improves correctness on ambiguity-sensitive problems and reduces confidently-wrong answers, with especially high stakes in clinical reasoning.
Related Work: Recent work shows ambiguity is linearly encoded and sparsely represented: linear probes decode ambiguity >90% while direct prompting fails (Trick or Neat, 2025), a handful of Ambiguity-Encoding Neurons carry the signal and steering them shifts behavior from answering to abstention (Sparse Neurons Carry Strong Signals of Question Ambiguity, 2025), models 'overcommit to deterministic interpretations' (Bridging Philosophical Foundations, 2025), can track syntactic uncertainty in generation but bias toward one reading under greedy decoding (The LM Understood the Prompt was Ambiguous, 2021), and can even exploit ambiguity loopholes (LMs Identify Ambiguities and Exploit Loopholes, 2025). All existing work treats ambiguity as a detection/abstention target (answer vs. clarify) or a static representational property. None ask whether, during multi-step reasoning, the model maintains MULTIPLE interpretation branches in parallel versus prematurely pruning to one, whether branch-count is a per-step trajectory that collapses before evidence warrants it, or whether causally keeping branches alive (rather than abstaining) improves task correctness. My prior proposals covered answer-commitment timing under word order and difficulty-gated signals, but none address interpretation-branch maintenance under semantic ambiguity. We uniquely reframe ambiguity handling from abstention to parallel-hypothesis maintenance, with a Location + Causal Intervention account and a high-stakes clinical instance.
Abstract: Real questions are often ambiguous, admitting several valid interpretations, yet large language models tend to answer with a single confident reading. Prior work frames this as a detection problem (should the model abstain or ask to clarify?) and shows ambiguity is linearly encoded and steerable. We ask a different, dynamic question: while an LLM reasons through an ambiguous problem, does it keep the competing interpretations alive in parallel, or does it silently collapse to one branch too early, then reason confidently down it? We hypothesize premature disambiguation: the model commits to a single reading before it has the evidence to select one, and this collapse is a proximal cause of confidently-wrong answers on ambiguity-sensitive tasks. We define a per-step interpretation-branch signal read from hidden states and test three claims. First, branch collapse is real and premature: the number of live interpretation branches drops sharply early in reasoning, often before any disambiguating cue appears. Second, the branch signal is diagnostic: how early and how completely the model collapses predicts final-answer errors on genuinely ambiguous items, beyond confidence and entropy. Third, it is causally fixable: inducing the model to keep multiple branches alive (via a branch-maintenance intervention and by steering a located branch-diversity direction) improves correctness and reduces confidently-wrong answers relative to no-intervention, abstention prompting, and 'consider alternatives' prompting. We evaluate on lexical, syntactic, and scope-ambiguity reasoning across several open-weight models, plus a high-stakes clinical instance where an ambiguous symptom description silently collapses to one diagnosis. Our work reframes ambiguity handling as parallel-hypothesis maintenance and offers an interpretable failure signal and a training-free intervention.
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use five frozen open-weight models -- Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights on frozen hidden states. Decoding is greedy for primary conditions and temperature 0.7 for sampled conditions, each sampled run over seeds 0, 1, 2. Effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap CIs over 1000 item-level resamples; behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts (1|model)+(1|item). A "live interpretation branch" is a distinct reading the model is still pursuing; "premature disambiguation" means collapse to one branch before any disambiguating cue appears.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Branch collapse is real and occurs before disambiguating evidence): Tests whether the number of live interpretation branches drops early, before the resolving cue. Data: an ambiguity-reasoning battery of 250 items per type where the ambiguity is decision-relevant -- (a) lexical ambiguity (a key word has two answer-changing senses), (b) syntactic/attachment ambiguity (PP-attachment, coordination scope), (c) quantifier/scope ambiguity -- 750 ambiguous items plus 250 matched unambiguous controls (one reading only) for selectivity, adapted where possible from AmbiEnt/AmbAdv-style ambiguity datasets and templated construction; each ambiguous item places its disambiguating cue at a known late position and carries a labeled correct behavior (hedge when unresolvable, single reading when a later cue resolves it) and a premature-commit lure (the answer if the model locks onto the more frequent reading early). 250/type is the smallest sample giving stable collapse-position estimates under sampling-based branch counting within budget. Branch signal: at each step we sample N=10 continuations (temperature 0.7), cluster them by which interpretation they pursue (embedding + manual-validated rubric), giving a per-step live-branch count / interpretation entropy. Decisive metric first: the gap between collapse position (first step where a single branch dominates, entropy below threshold) and the resolving-cue position, on ambiguous items; secondary: whether collapse is toward the higher-frequency reading, versus unambiguous controls that should start single-branch. Convincing result: mean collapse position precedes the cue position by a reliable margin on ambiguous items (CI on the difference excludes 0 and is directional), collapse is biased toward the frequent reading, and unambiguous controls show no premature multi-branch collapse. Indecision band: a collapse-minus-cue position difference whose CI overlaps 0 (within about +/-0.5 steps) means we cannot show prematurity. Negative result: collapse at or after the cue means the model resolves only on evidence -- well-calibrated, not premature -- refuting H1.

Experiment 2 (H1 -- A locatable branch signal, cross-validated behaviorally and representationally): Tests that branch diversity is readable from hidden states. Data: the same battery, split 70/30 by item. A linear probe (only probe trainable) on per-step hidden states decodes which interpretation(s) are active and estimates a branch-diversity score (per-layer held-out AUROC), validated against the sampling-based branch proxy from Experiment 1. Decisive metric first: held-out probe AUROC for the active-interpretation set; secondary: rank correlation between probe branch-diversity and the sampling branch count. Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.70 and Spearman rho >= 0.4 agreement with the behavioral proxy (CIs exclude 0). Indecision band: AUROC 0.55-0.65 or agreement rho 0.2-0.35 means the cheap probe cannot stand in for the behavioral measure. Negative result: chance AUROC means no locatable branch signal, and later steering (Experiment 5) is uninterpretable.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- Earliness/completeness of collapse is diagnostic of error beyond confidence and entropy): Tests whether collapse predicts final error. Data: the same items. Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC for final-answer error predicted from collapse earliness and completeness; secondary: delta-AUROC over verbalized confidence, token entropy, and a semantic-uncertainty baseline. Convincing result: collapse-based AUROC >= 0.65 exceeding the best baseline by >= 0.05 (CI excludes 0), specifically predicting confidently-wrong answers. Indecision band: delta-AUROC over baselines within +/-0.03 means collapse adds no diagnostic value. Negative result: AUROC ~ 0.5 refutes H2.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- Branch-maintenance improves correctness and reduces confidently-wrong answers): Tests the behavioral intervention. Data: the 750 ambiguous items plus 250 unambiguous controls. Systems: no-intervention; abstention/clarify prompting (prior framing); generic "consider alternative interpretations" prompting; and structured Branch-Maintenance (enumerate both readings and carry them in parallel until a resolving cue, then commit); a length-matched control equalizes tokens with the generic-alternatives arm. Decisive metric first: task correctness on ambiguous items, primary contrast Branch-Maintenance minus generic-alternatives; secondary: confidently-wrong rate, appropriate-hedge rate on truly-unresolvable items, and cost on unambiguous controls. Convincing result: Branch-Maintenance beats generic-alternatives and abstention prompting by >= 3 points correctness on ambiguous items (CI excludes 0), especially on premature-lure-prone items, lowers confidently-wrong rate, and costs <= 2 points on unambiguous controls. Indecision band: within +/-2 points of the generic-alternatives arm means parallel maintenance adds nothing beyond extra deliberation. Negative result: no gain over "consider alternatives" refutes H3's intervention claim.

Experiment 5 (H3 -- Steering a branch-diversity direction causally delays collapse): Tests the mechanism. Data: matched multi-branch-minus-collapsed-branch step contrasts yield a difference-in-means "branch-diversity" direction at the best probe layer. Systems: plus-direction steering (delay collapse), minus-direction (force early collapse), random-direction of matched norm, no-steer. Decisive metric first: change in premature-lure error rate under plus-direction versus random-direction steering; secondary: minus-direction induced error, dose-response, whether per-item branch-diversity increase mediates the correctness gain (Spearman), and specificity (unambiguous-item accuracy within 1 point, fluency preserved). Convincing result: plus-direction steering reduces premature-lure errors by >= 3 points over random-direction (CI excludes 0) with monotonic dose-response and preserved unambiguous accuracy, minus-direction increases them, and branch-diversity change mediates correctness. Indecision band: effects within +/-2 points of random-direction leave the direction unproven; the behavioral Experiment 4 then stands alone. Negative result: no steerable effect means branch diversity is not a causal lever.

Experiment 6 (H3 -- High-stakes clinical instance): Tests premature collapse to the common diagnosis. Data: 300 clinical vignettes adapted from MedQA (USMLE, 12,723 questions) and constructed cases where an ambiguous symptom description supports two plausible diagnoses until a later detail resolves it; 300 supports paired contrasts under expert spot-checking. Systems: no-intervention, Branch-Maintenance, and branch-diversity plus-direction steering. Decisive metric first: confident-misdiagnosis rate on resolve-late cases under no-intervention versus the two mitigations; secondary: overall diagnostic accuracy. Convincing result: the model prematurely collapses to the common diagnosis at baseline and both mitigations cut confident misdiagnosis by >= 5 points (CIs exclude 0). Indecision band: mitigation effects within +/-2 points are inconclusive for high-stakes transfer. Negative result: no baseline premature collapse or no mitigation effect bounds the claim to benign tasks.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The behavioral branch proxy via sampling is expensive and noisy; we mitigate with moderate N, clustering validation, and cross-checking against the cheaper representational probe. (2) 'Premature' requires distinguishing collapse-before-cue from legitimate early resolution; we control this by placing the disambiguating cue at a known late position and comparing collapse position to cue position, and by using truly-unresolvable items where no early commitment is warranted. (3) Instruction-tuned models may already hedge or abstain heavily, muting collapse; we include base variants, calibrate item difficulty, and measure the confidently-wrong rate specifically. (4) Branch-Maintenance prompting could help simply by adding tokens/deliberation; the 'consider alternatives' and length-matched controls isolate genuine parallel-maintenance from mere extra thinking. (5) The branch-diversity direction may entangle with generic uncertainty rather than interpretation multiplicity; mitigated by matched multi- vs single-branch contrasts, random-direction steering, unambiguous-control specificity, and comparison to the existing ambiguity/verbal-uncertainty linear features. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (models keep branches alive or collapse only after cues) is itself informative, showing LLM ambiguity handling is well-calibrated rather than prematurely committing. (8) The parallel-hypothesis framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not a claim of human-like processing.

Name: morphological_role_scaffolding
Title: Case Closed: Does Overt Morphological Role-Marking Scaffold an LLM's Relational Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: A language's morphological role-marking (e.g., explicit case marking that tags each argument's role directly on the word) acts as a built-in scaffold for an LLM's relational reasoning: reasoning about role-sensitive problems framed in a morphologically transparent, case-marking language yields more robust argument-role binding, better resistance to word-order perturbation, and fewer role-confusion errors than the same content in a morphologically poor, word-order-reliant language like English, and this benefit is mediated by a locatable, steerable role-binding representation.
Related Work: Prior work characterizes morphological complexity information-theoretically (Productivity and Predictability, 2019; Processing-Oriented Inflectional Complexity, 2019), shows LLMs encode morphology in middle layers and that irregular-morphology languages benefit from more data (Tokenization and Morphology, 2024; LINSPECTOR, 2020), and shows LLMs reuse shared syntactic circuits across languages but add language-specific components for language-specific morphology (The Same But Different, 2024). Separately, 'When Less Language is More' (2025) shows ablating language-specific components improves multilingual reasoning, treating morphology/language as noise. My prior proposals covered word-order typology (answer-commitment), tokenization granularity, lexical gaps, evidentiality, tense, and counterfactual mood, but NONE address morphological role-marking (case) as a functional scaffold for relational reasoning. No prior work asks whether overt morphological role-marking causally improves argument-role binding and relational-reasoning robustness, tests whether it makes reasoning resistant to word-order scrambling, or links this to a locatable role-binding representation. We uniquely reframe morphology from a modeling nuisance into a controllable reasoning resource, with a Location + Causal Intervention account and a high-stakes clinical instance.
Abstract: Human languages divide labor between word order and morphology to signal who did what to whom: English relies on word order ('the dog bit the man'), while case-marking languages tag each argument's role directly on the word, freeing word order. We ask whether this typological choice shapes machine intelligence: does overt morphological role-marking act as a built-in scaffold that makes an LLM's relational reasoning more robust? We construct role-sensitive reasoning problems (agent/patient tracking, multi-participant event chains, transitive relational inference) and render each, with content held constant, in a morphologically poor, word-order-reliant language (English) versus morphologically transparent, case-marking languages (e.g., Turkish, Russian, Finnish). Our central prediction is a morphology-scaffolding effect: role-marked framing yields fewer role-confusion errors and, critically, greater robustness to word-order scrambling that would break a purely order-based reasoner, whereas English framing collapses under scrambling. We further predict the benefit is largest exactly when role assignment is hard (many participants, non-canonical order). Mechanistically, we test whether overt case-marking strengthens a locatable role-binding representation: a probe decoding which entity fills which role should be more accurate and more scramble-invariant under case-marking, this representational robustness should mediate the behavioral gain item-by-item, and steering a located role-binding direction should induce or cancel the scaffolding effect. We evaluate across several open-weight multilingual models, plus a high-stakes clinical instance where scrambled or morphologically ambiguous phrasing of 'drug X interacts with drug Y' silently flips the reasoned direction. Our work reframes morphology from a modeling nuisance into a controllable scaffold for relational intelligence.
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use five frozen open-weight multilingual models -- Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights on frozen hidden states. Decoding is greedy for primary conditions and temperature 0.7 for sampled conditions, each sampled run over seeds 0, 1, 2. Effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap CIs over 1000 item-level resamples; behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts (1|model)+(1|item). All cross-lingual analyses are accuracy-stratified so that the morphology effect is separated from a language's general resource competence. "Role-confusion lure" is the answer obtained if agent/patient (or an asymmetric relation's direction) is swapped.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Overt case-marking lowers role-confusion errors, most when role assignment is hard): Tests the core scaffolding effect with content held constant. Data: a role-sensitive battery of 250 items per family -- (a) agent/patient tracking over 2-5 participants, (b) multi-participant event chains (A gave B to C, C passed it to D... query final holder), (c) transitive relational inference over asymmetric relations -- 750 items, plus 250 matched role-symmetric controls (relations where role order does not matter) for selectivity; each item has a labeled correct answer and a labeled role-confusion lure. Each item is rendered, content held constant and back-translation-checked, in English (morphologically poor, order-reliant) and in Turkish, Russian, and Finnish (overt case marking). 250/family supports stable language_type x difficulty estimates within budget. Decisive metric first: role-confusion lure rate (and accuracy) under case-marking versus English from mixed-effects regression lure_rate ~ language_type * difficulty + (1|model)+(1|item), accuracy-stratified; secondary: the widening of the gap as role-assignment difficulty rises (more participants, non-canonical order). Convincing result: case-marking framing lowers the role-confusion lure rate relative to English by a reliable margin (CI excludes 0) that grows with difficulty, holding at matched competence. Indecision band: a language_type effect within +/-2 points (CI overlapping 0) after accuracy-stratification means no morphology advantage is detectable above resource differences. Negative result: no case-marking advantage means relational reasoning is order-agnostic and content-driven, refuting H1 and dissociating LLMs from the human labor-division account.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- Case-marking gives robustness to word-order scrambling that English lacks): The sharpest test. Data: the same items; we permute the surface order of arguments within each item. Under case marking the morphology still uniquely determines roles (meaning preserved, native-speaker-verified on a sample), while English scrambling destroys or flips role cues. Decisive metric first: the language_type x scramble interaction on accuracy from mixed-effects regression accuracy ~ language_type * scramble + (1|model)+(1|item); secondary: where scrambling errors concentrate (should be on the role-confusion lure in English). Convincing result: case-marking framing shows a small accuracy drop under scrambling (<= 5 points) while English collapses (>= 15-point drop), yielding a large, reliable interaction (CI excludes 0) with English errors concentrated on the role-confusion lure. Indecision band: an interaction whose CI corresponds to a between-language drop difference within +/-3 points means scrambling robustness is not distinguishable between framings. Negative result: equal collapse under scrambling in both framings means overt morphology does not scaffold role binding, refuting H2 (the central novel claim).

Experiment 3 (H1/H2 -- High-stakes clinical direction-flip instance): Tests whether English non-canonical/scrambled phrasing silently flips a clinical causal direction. Data: 300 drug-interaction / causal-direction vignettes ("drug X potentiates drug Y", dosage-adjustment directionality) adapted from a curated drug-interaction knowledge base and constructed cases where the reasoned direction matters; rendered in English and case-marking languages, with 2-5 interacting entities; 300 supports paired contrasts under expert spot-checking. Decisive metric first: direction-flip rate (inferred direction reversed from ground truth) under English scrambled/non-canonical phrasing versus case-marked framing; secondary: scaling of the flip rate with number of interacting entities. Convincing result: English scrambled phrasing raises the direction-flip rate while case-marked framing preserves direction, a reliable gap (CI excludes 0) that grows with entity count. Indecision band: a flip-rate gap within +/-2 points is inconclusive for high-stakes transfer. Negative result: no flip-rate difference bounds the scaffolding claim to benign benchmarks.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- A locatable role-binding representation is stronger and more scramble-invariant under case-marking): Tests the mechanism's representational side. Data: the battery from Experiments 1-2, split 70/30 by item. A linear probe (only probe trainable) on mid-layer hidden states at the query position decodes which entity fills the queried role (per-layer held-out AUROC). Decisive metric first: probe role-decoding AUROC under case-marking versus English, and its scramble-invariance (AUROC drop under scrambling); secondary: per-item mediation -- whether probe role-decodability and its scramble-invariance predict per-item accuracy/lure-rate (Spearman). Convincing result: role-decoding AUROC is higher and markedly more scramble-invariant under case-marking (AUROC-drop difference CI excludes 0), and per-item decodability predicts accuracy (rho >= 0.2, CI excludes 0). Indecision band: an AUROC-invariance difference within +/-0.03 means the representation is not demonstrably more robust under morphology. Negative result: equal probe robustness across framings means the behavioral effect (if any) is not carried by a morphology-strengthened role-binding representation.

Experiment 5 (H3 -- Steering the role-binding direction rescues and induces role confusion): Tests causality. Data: a difference-in-means "role-binding" direction from correct-role-bound-minus-role-confused contrasts at the best probe layer. Systems: plus-direction steering under scrambled English (rescue), minus-direction under case-marking framing (induce confusion despite morphology), random-direction of matched norm, no-steer. Decisive metric first: accuracy recovery under plus-direction steering of scrambled English versus random-direction; secondary: induced lure-rate increase under minus-direction on case-marked items, dose-response, and specificity (role-symmetric-control accuracy within 1 point, fluency preserved). Convincing result: plus-direction steering recovers scrambled-English accuracy toward case-marking levels (>= 3-point gain over random-direction, CI excludes 0), minus-direction induces role confusion despite overt case marking, both with monotonic dose-response and preserved role-symmetric-control accuracy. Indecision band: steering effects within +/-2 points of random-direction leave the direction unproven; the behavioral scrambling test (Experiment 2) then stands alone. Negative result: no steerable rescue/induction means the role-binding direction is not causal.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Case-marking languages may be lower-resource for these models, confounding morphology with competence; mitigated by accuracy-stratified metrics, back-translation checks, and the content-matched steering intervention that isolates the role-binding representation from language. (2) Tokenization may fragment case suffixes, weakening the morphological signal; we test multiple case-marking languages/models and report robustness, and the within-English scramble test (which needs no cross-lingual comparison) is a clean primary probe of the word-order-reliance failure mode. (3) The scrambling stress test requires that scrambled case-marked sentences stay unambiguous and English scrambling genuinely disrupts roles; we validate both with native speakers on a sample and design canonical/non-canonical orders carefully. (4) Instruction-tuned models may reason robustly regardless of framing, yielding ceiling effects; we increase participant count, use non-canonical orders, and calibrate difficulty to mid-range. (5) The role-binding direction may entangle with generic difficulty rather than role assignment per se; mitigated by matched role-bound vs role-confused contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and role-symmetric-control specificity checks. (6) Effects may be small or model/language-specific; we test multiple models and languages and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (morphological role-marking gives no robustness advantage) is itself informative: it would show LLM relational reasoning is order-agnostic and content-driven rather than scaffolded by surface morphology, dissociating LLMs from the human labor-division account. (8) The morphology-as-scaffold framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like processing.

Name: canonicalization_convergence
Title: Mental Paraphrase: Do LLMs Normalize a Problem Toward a Canonical Form Before Reasoning, and Do Failures Come From Not Getting There?
Short Hypothesis: Before reasoning, an LLM internally normalizes a problem's varied surface phrasings toward a shared canonical representation ('mental paraphrase'); reasoning errors on awkward or unfamiliar surface forms are caused by incomplete convergence to that canonical form rather than by the reasoning steps themselves, and the degree of convergence is a readable, causal signal that predicts correctness and can be causally restored by injecting the canonical representation.
Related Work: Prior work documents that LLMs are brittle to surface form: subtle rephrasings change math solve rates (Paraphrase and Solve / SCoP, 2024), reasoning traces are robust to some CoT interventions but not style-invariant and paraphrasing shortens traces and harms accuracy (Are Reasoning LLMs Robust to Interventions on Their CoT?, 2026), and CoT is often unfaithful (Measuring Faithfulness in CoT, 2023). Representation studies show reasoning representations converge across languages when reasoning succeeds (Under the Shadow of Babel, 2025), that NMT paraphrase-invariance is largely shallow (Neurons Invariant to Sentence Structural Changes, 2022), and that abstract concept vectors exist but are not always output-invariant (Concept Vectors, 2025; Abstract Activation Spaces, 2026). Content-effect work steers a 'validity vs plausibility' direction to debias reasoning (How LMs Conflate Validity with Plausibility, 2025; K-CAST, 2025). ALL of these are either (a) behavioral surface-form robustness studies with no internal mechanism, or (b) steering of a content/validity concept. NONE propose that the model performs an internal canonicalization step that maps diverse phrasings toward a shared normal form before reasoning, that reasoning failure is caused by INCOMPLETE convergence to that canonical form, that per-item convergence is a diagnostic signal of correctness, or that injecting the canonical representation causally rescues hard-phrasing errors. My prior proposals covered word-order, morphology, tokenization granularity, lexical gaps, and grammatical-mood effects, but none address surface-form-invariant canonicalization as a locatable, causal computation. We uniquely reframe paraphrase brittleness from a behavioral quirk into a mechanistic canonicalization-convergence account with a Location + Causal Intervention strategy and a high-stakes clinical instance.
Abstract: Large language models solve the same problem at different rates depending only on how it is worded, yet why remains unclear. We propose a mechanistic account: before reasoning, the model performs a 'mental paraphrase', normalizing a problem's diverse surface forms toward a shared canonical representation, and reasoning failures on awkward or unfamiliar phrasings arise because the model never fully reaches that canonical form. We make three claims. First, canonicalization is real and graded: across paraphrase clusters (many wordings of one problem), the internal representations converge toward a common form in intermediate layers, and convergence is stronger for the phrasings the model solves correctly. Second, convergence is diagnostic: per-item distance from the paraphrase cluster's canonical representation predicts whether that phrasing will be solved, beyond confidence and entropy, and pinpoints which surface forms are 'lost in translation' before any reasoning error appears. Third, convergence is causal, not incidental: patching the canonical representation (derived from easy, frequent phrasings) into the model's processing of a hard phrasing rescues correctness, and steering along a located 'canonicalization' direction moves reasoning accuracy up or down. We test these on math, logic, and multi-hop QA with controlled paraphrase clusters spanning register, syntax, and verbosity across several open-weight models, plus a high-stakes clinical instance where a benign rephrasing of a case description silently degrades diagnostic accuracy through failed canonicalization. Our work reframes paraphrase brittleness as incomplete internal normalization and offers an interpretable pre-reasoning failure signal and a training-free rescue.
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use five frozen open-weight models -- Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights on frozen hidden states. Decoding is greedy for primary conditions and temperature 0.7 for sampled conditions, each sampled run over seeds 0, 1, 2. Effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap CIs over 1000 item-level resamples; behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts. "Canonicalization convergence" means the degree to which the internal representations of many wordings of one problem approach a shared form before reasoning; the "Convergence Score" is negative distance from a phrasing's pre-reasoning representation to its cluster's canonical (frequent/terse-formal) centroid at the layer of maximal within-cluster convergence.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Canonicalization is real, graded, and stronger for correctly solved phrasings): Tests within-cluster convergence and its link to correctness. Data: for each base problem we build a cluster of 8-12 meaning-preserving paraphrases spanning controlled axes (register formal/colloquial, syntax simple/embedded, verbosity terse/padded, voice active/passive), over 200 base problems from the GSM8K test split (1,319 available), 200 from the MATH test split (5,000 available), 150 synthetic deductive-logic chains (depth 2-6, auto-checkable), and 150 from the 2WikiMultiHopQA dev set (12,576 available), 700 clusters / roughly 5,600-8,400 phrasings; paraphrases are generated by templated transforms plus an LLM paraphraser and meaning-preservation is verified by back-translation and human spot-check on a 10% sample. 700 clusters gives enough within-cluster behavioral variance for stable convergence estimates within budget. We extract pre-reasoning hidden states at the end-of-problem position per phrasing per layer, compute within-cluster dispersion by layer and each phrasing's distance to the canonical centroid, controlling for length and word-overlap by regression. Decisive metric first: within-cluster representational dispersion as a function of layer (does it fall to a minimum in intermediate layers?) and the Convergence Score difference between correctly and incorrectly solved phrasings; secondary: the layer of maximal convergence per model. Convincing result: dispersion shows a clear intermediate-layer minimum and correctly solved phrasings have reliably higher Convergence Score than incorrect ones (CI excludes 0) after controlling for length/word-overlap. Indecision band: a correct-minus-incorrect Convergence difference whose CI lies within +/-0.05 standardized units means convergence is not graded by correctness. Negative result: flat dispersion across layers or no correctness link means there is no canonicalization computation, refuting H1.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- Convergence is diagnostic of solve probability before reasoning): Tests pre-reasoning error prediction. Data: the same clusters, split 70/30 by cluster. Decisive metric first: from mixed-effects logistic regression correct ~ Convergence + length + word_overlap + (1|cluster)+(1|model), the Convergence coefficient's significance beyond shallow features; secondary: held-out AUROC of a probe on Convergence features for predicting correctness versus verbalized confidence, token entropy, and per-token surprisal baselines. Convincing result: Convergence retains a reliable positive coefficient beyond length/word-overlap (CI excludes 0) and its AUROC exceeds the best baseline by >= 0.05, measured before any reasoning tokens. Indecision band: a Convergence coefficient CI overlapping 0, or delta-AUROC within +/-0.03, means convergence carries no diagnostic value beyond shallow similarity. Negative result: no predictive power refutes H2.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- Patching the canonical representation causally rescues hard-phrasing errors): Tests the causal rescue. Data: hard phrasings the model fails, paired with an easy/canonical phrasing of the SAME problem. We cache the pre-reasoning representation from the canonical phrasing and patch it into the hard-phrasing forward pass at the convergence layer. Controls: patch from a DIFFERENT problem's canonical representation (specificity), patch a random-matched representation, and no-patch baseline; we verify no answer tokens are present in the patched pre-reasoning representation (rules out answer-leakage). Decisive metric first: accuracy recovery on failed hard phrasings under same-problem canonical patching versus no-patch; secondary: same-problem versus cross-problem/random patching. Convincing result: same-problem canonical patching recovers accuracy by >= 8 points (CI excludes 0) while cross-problem and random patching do not (within 2 points of no-patch). Indecision band: a same-problem recovery within +/-3 points, or a same-versus-cross gap within +/-3 points, means patching does not selectively restore canonicalization. Negative result: no selective recovery, or equal recovery from cross-problem patches, refutes the causal canonicalization-bottleneck claim (and would indicate answer-leakage if cross-problem also rescues).

Experiment 4 (H3 -- Steering a canonicalization direction moves accuracy): Tests the mechanism's generality. Data: matched converged-minus-non-converged phrasing contrasts (content matched) yield a difference-in-means "canonicalization" direction at the convergence layer.
